parts.description: A matte black cast-iron teapot with a rounded bulbous body, short spout, fitted lid, and arched metal handle wrapped in tan woven material.
parts.reasoning: The object appears to be an empty cast-iron teapot/tetsubin with a hollow rounded body, lid, knob, spout, and a relatively thin arched handle. The dominant exterior/contact material is black enamel-coated or oxidized cast iron; the tan wrap on the handle is a minor external material and should not drive root-level friction or density. A typical teapot of this apparent size is approximately 0.17–0.20 m in body diameter, 0.10–0.13 m body height, about 0.23–0.26 m long including the spout, and about 0.20–0.24 m tall including the handle. Empty mass is estimated at about 1.6 kg, consistent with a 2.5–3.5 mm cast-iron shell plus lid, spout, and handle hardware. The listed density is the material density of cast iron, about 7200 kg/m^3; however, for Isaac Sim it is better to assign the mass explicitly because using this density on a closed convex hull of the entire teapot would overestimate mass due to the hollow interior. A practical effective density for an automatically mass-computed single closed collision envelope would be much lower, roughly 300–700 kg/m^3 depending on the chosen collision volume. Static friction is estimated at 0.55 and dynamic friction at 0.43 for rough enamel/cast iron against common tabletops or metal fixtures. Restitution is set low at 0.25 because the hollow cast-iron body is hard but not very elastic in practical impacts, and low bounce improves stable resting contacts. For collision geometry, a single convex hull is not recommended because it would fill the handle arch, spout gap, and body concavities. Convex decomposition or manually authored primitive hulls/capsules are recommended: 1–3 hulls for the rounded body, a shallow cylinder/hull for the lid, a sphere or capsule for the knob, tapered hulls for the spout, and capsule-like hulls for the arched handle. SDF mesh collision is only needed if the open spout/mouth or exact concave handle clearance must be physically accessible; otherwise convex decomposition is faster and more stable. Contact offset around 0.004 m is appropriate for a 20 cm object with small curved features; rest offset should remain 0.0 m to avoid visible floating. CCD is normally not required for a slowly handled heavy tabletop object, but should be enabled if the teapot is thrown, dropped from height with thin spout/handle collision enabled, or moved faster than several centimeters per physics step. Compliant contacts should be disabled for this non-deformable cast-iron asset; if contact jitter appears, increase solver iterations rather than softening the material.
